To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the presence of a monophosphoryl group at the 5'-end of a substrate RNA increases the activity and specificity of the RNase E and the RNase G ribonucleases; and 2) the catalytic enhancement by 5'-terminal monophosphorylylation requires the formation of multimers of these enzymes.
5'-monophasphorylation enhances the catalytic potency and cleavage specificity of the RNase E and the RNase G endonucleases, and that this requires protein multimerization.
the 5'-monphosphorylated RNA substrates are cleaved more efficiently by the RNase E and G than the 5' triphosphorylated or hydroxyl RNA substrates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms by which RNase E and other RNA degradosomes regulate RNA processing, degradation and gene expression in bacteria.
the mechanisms by which 5' end phosphorylation influences the activity of the RNase E and G enzymes, which are essential in the processing and degradation of bacterial mRNAs.
the molecular basis of catalytic regulation by 5' monomethylated RNA in Escherichian coli.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of a monophosphate on the 5' terminus of RNA can accelerate RNA cleavage by multimeric RNases E and G, and that this effect requires the formation of multimers of these enzymes.
5'-end phosphorylation of RNAs is a mechanism for regulating the catalytic activity of RNase G and RNase E.
the presence of the 5'-terminal phosphate group is required for the catalytic activation of RNase E by its own multimeric state.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the 5' phosphate is an allosteric activator of the RNase E and G catalytic sites.
RNase E is a highly efficient RNA degradase that has evolved to recognize and cleave the 5' ends of RNA.
5'-end phosphorylation is a critical determinant of RNA cleavage by RNase E, and that RNase E can discriminate between RNA substrata on the basis of the phosphorylation state of the 5' ends.
The main takeaway from our work is that
5'-mononucleotidylation is a potent signal in the regulation of RNA metabolism.
the catalytic properties of multimeric enzymes can be modulated by the chemical properties of their substrates.
the 5' monophasphoryl group is an allosteric activator of RNase E, and that this activation requires the formation of multimers.
